old: Large language models can describe political controversies accurately while omitting relevant perspectives. We test whether they recover fewer documented perspectives on Serbian controversies than on structurally matched topics from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) settings. The benchmark pairs eight Serbian controversies with WEIRD counterparts; each of the 16 topics has five reference perspectives documented in surveys, polling, referendum results, research, or public debate. Thirteen LLMs each generated five perspectives per topic in English, and five LLM judges from other developers matched each output to a reference or returned no match. Mean recall was 0.581 on WEIRD topics and 0.594 on Serbian topics. The mean WEIRD-minus-Serbian difference across the eight pairs was $-1.3$ percentage points (95\% CI: $-10.3$ to $7.7$), and an exact one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test found no evidence for the hypothesised WEIRD advantage ($p=0.680$). Differences between individual pairs ($-16.9$ to $+19.1$ points) were much larger than the pooled difference. Judges agreed similarly on both sets of topics (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.77$), but agreement does not establish accuracy. Coverage was incomplete in both settings, and the result does not establish equivalent coverage.
new: Large language models can describe political controversies accurately while omitting relevant perspectives. We test whether they recover fewer documented perspectives on Serbian controversies than on structurally matched topics from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) settings. The benchmark pairs eight Serbian controversies with WEIRD counterparts; each of the 16 topics has five reference perspectives documented in surveys, polling, referendum results, research, or public debate. Thirteen LLMs each generated five perspectives per topic in English, and five LLM judges from other developers matched each output to a reference or returned no match. Mean recall was 0.581 on WEIRD topics and 0.594 on Serbian topics. The mean WEIRD-minus-Serbian difference across the eight pairs was $-1.3$ percentage points (95\% $t$-based CI: $-10.3$ to $7.7$), and an exact one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test found no evidence for the hypothesised WEIRD advantage ($p=0.680$). Differences between individual pairs ($-16.9$ to $+19.1$ points) were much larger than the pooled difference. Inter-judge agreement was similar across the two settings (pooled Fleiss' $\kappa=0.77$), but agreement does not establish accuracy. Coverage was incomplete in both settings, and the result does not establish equivalent coverage.

old: The base panel contains Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, and Kimi K2.6. old: The primary comparison rests on eight topic pairs whose WEIRD-minus-Serbian differences vary widely (SD 10.7 percentage points). With eight resampling units, the percentile pair-bootstrap interval ($-8.1$ to $5.8$ points) is likely to be too narrow; a $t$-based interval is $-10.3$ to $7.7$ points, and the one-sided 95\% upper bound is $5.9$ points. The data therefore argue against a WEIRD advantage much larger than about six points for pairs like these, but cannot exclude smaller advantages or moderate differences favouring Serbian topics. Given this between-pair variation, a one-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ would detect a five-point WEIRD advantage only about one time in three, and reaches 80\% power only for advantages of about 10.5 points. We therefore report no detectable WEIRD advantage, not equality between settings.
new: The primary comparison rests on eight topic pairs whose WEIRD-minus-Serbian differences vary widely (SD 10.7 percentage points). With eight resampling units, the percentile pair-bootstrap interval ($-8.1$ to $5.8$ points) may have limited coverage accuracy; a $t$-based interval is $-10.3$ to $7.7$ points, and the one-sided 95\% upper bound is $5.9$ points. Under the independent-pair and $t$-interval assumptions, the one-sided bound is approximately six points. It is conditional on these assumptions and the selected benchmark; it does not establish a general upper bound on cultural disparities. Smaller WEIRD advantages and moderate differences favouring Serbian topics remain compatible with the interval. An illustrative sensitivity calculation for a one-sided one-sample $t$-test at $\alpha=0.05$, assuming normally distributed pair-level differences and using the observed SD, gives approximately 32\% power for a five-point WEIRD advantage and 80\% power for an advantage of about 10.5 points. These values describe the $t$-test calculation, not the exact Wilcoxon procedure used for the primary test. We therefore report no detectable WEIRD advantage, not equality between settings.
reason: Qualify the bound and correctly identify the power calculation; preserve reported numerical values.

The $t$-based interval for the mean gap uses the eight $\Delta_p$ values (SD $0.107$, SE $0.038$) with $t_{7}$ quantiles, giving $[-0.103, 0.077]$; the one-sided 95\% upper bound is $0.059$. The $t$-based interval for the mean gap uses the eight $\Delta_p$ values (SD $0.107$, SE $0.038$) with $t_{7}$ quantiles, giving $[-0.103, 0.077]$; the one-sided 95\% upper bound is $0.059$. The random-number generator is initialized with seed $42$. All $\binom{13}{2}=78$ model pairs use this procedure, and the resulting raw $p$-values are adjusted jointly using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. This is a Monte Carlo paired sign-flip test, not exhaustive enumeration of all $2^{16}$ sign patterns.

The individual-topic sign-flip procedure assumes sign exchangeability at the topic level and does not preserve the matched pairs. To assess sensitivity to this choice, we also form eight pair-level contrasts,
\[
x_p=\frac{R_{a,p}^{\mathrm W}+R_{a,p}^{\mathrm S}}{2}
    -\frac{R_{b,p}^{\mathrm W}+R_{b,p}^{\mathrm S}}{2},
\]
and enumerate all $2^8=256$ sign assignments using their mean as the statistic. Two-sided tail comparisons allow a numerical tolerance of $10^{-12}$, and Benjamini--Hochberg correction again covers all $78$ model comparisons. This procedure assumes sign-exchangeable pair-level contrasts and preserves the original mean difference. As a numerical check, exhaustive enumeration of the $2^{16}$ individual-topic sign patterns still yields 15 adjusted significant comparisons, whereas the pair-blocked procedure yields none (minimum adjusted $p=0.087$). The discrepancy therefore reflects the inferential unit rather than Monte Carlo sampling alone. The pair-blocked results qualify the individual-topic findings; neither procedure establishes equivalence between models.
